---
title: "Testing the apps you already built"
---

You know your salon app works because you typed three names into it, clicked
Serve next three times, and watched the line empty out. Every change you make
from now on costs you that walk-through again. This chapter hands it to
Playwright. It starts with a recorder that writes the first draft while you
click, and it ends with a computer at GitHub that repeats everything after
every push.

## The recorder writes the first draft {#sec-testing-apps-codegen}

1. Open `coursework/hairdresser`, the salon app from the queues chapter, and
   start it with `npm start`.

2. Leave it running and open a second terminal in the same folder:

   ```text
   npx playwright codegen http://localhost:5173/
   ```

   Two windows open. On the left is your salon, on the right the Playwright
   Inspector with an empty code panel.

3. Click through one customer in the left window. Type `Mia` into First name,
   `Berger` into Last name, tick Long hair, click Add human, then click Serve
   next. Watch the right window fill up while you click.

4. Stop the recorder with Ctrl+C in the terminal. Here is what the Inspector
   collected:

   ```ts
   import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

   test('test', async ({ page }) => {
     await page.goto('http://localhost:5173/');
     await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'First name' }).click();
     await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'First name' }).fill('Mia');
     await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Last name' }).click();
     await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Last name' }).fill('Berger');
     await page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: 'Long hair' }).check();
     await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add human' }).click();
     await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Serve next' }).click();
   });
   ```

That is a real Playwright test, and it is not yet a test worth keeping. Read
it once and count what has to change.

**The test is called `test`.** The recorder does not know what you were
trying to prove. You do, so write the sentence.

**The address is hard-coded.** `playwright.config.ts` starts its own copy of
Vite on port 4173 and puts that address into `baseURL`, so `page.goto('/')`
lands on the right page every time. The recorded line points at the dev server
you happened to have open, and next week you will have a different app on that
port.

**There is a click before every `fill`.** You moved the cursor into the field,
so the recorder wrote it down. `fill` puts the cursor in the field itself, so
those three lines say nothing.

**Nothing is checked.** Codegen records what you did. It does not know what
you expected, and the whole point of a test is the expectation. Every
assertion in the file below is one you have to type.

The locators survive the cleanup with one change.
`getByRole('textbox', { name: 'First name' })` and `getByLabel('First name')`
find exactly the same input, because the accessible name of that textbox comes
from its `<label for>`. This course writes the shorter one.

Delete `e2e/add.e2e.ts`, which still tests the template's own page, and write
`e2e/salon.e2e.ts`:

```ts
import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test';

test('serves the customers in the order they arrived', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  await page.getByLabel('First name').fill('Mia');
  await page.getByLabel('Last name').fill('Berger');
  await page.getByLabel('Long hair').check();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add human' }).click();

  await page.getByLabel('Name', { exact: true }).fill('Rex');
  await page.getByLabel('Breed').fill('Beagle');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add dog' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByText('Now serving: 🧑 Mia Berger (long hair)')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByText('Next up: 🐕 Rex (Beagle)')).toBeVisible();

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Serve next' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByText('Now serving: 🐕 Rex (Beagle)')).toBeVisible();
});
```

The dog is in there because a queue with one customer proves nothing about
order. `check()` ticks the Long hair box and makes sure it really ends up
ticked, which a plain `click()` would not promise.

`{ exact: true }` on the dog's Name field is the one thing you cannot leave
out. Write `getByLabel('Name')` and the run stops before it clicks anything:

```text
Error: locator.fill: Error: strict mode violation: getByLabel('Name') resolved to 3 elements:
    1) <input type="text" id="humanFirstName"/> aka getByRole('textbox', { name: 'First name' })
    2) <input type="text" id="humanLastName"/> aka getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Last name' })
    3) <input type="text" id="dogName"/> aka getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Name', exact: true })
```

Playwright calls that **strict mode**, and it is on for every locator. A
locator that matches three elements is a question with three answers, and
Playwright refuses to guess which one you meant. `First name` and `Last name`
both contain the word `Name`, and `{ exact: true }` says you want the label
that reads exactly `Name`. The error even prints a locator that would work.

Run the file:

```text
npm run test:e2e
```

```text
Running 1 test using 1 worker

  ✓  1 e2e/salon.e2e.ts:3:1 › serves the customers in the order they arrived (368ms)

  1 passed (1.4s)
```

There is no `sleep` anywhere in that test, and there is no reason to add one.
Every locator action waits until the element is there and can be clicked, and
every `expect(locator)` keeps asking until the page agrees or five seconds are
up. Playwright calls this auto-waiting, and it is why an end-to-end suite can
be trusted on a slow machine.

## Error states are where a suite earns its keep {#sec-testing-apps-errors}

The happy flow is the part you test by hand anyway, because it is the part you
enjoy. The refusals are the part nobody clicks twice: the second letter cube in
a row, the empty name field, the warning that has to appear once and then stay
away. Those are also the parts that break quietly when you touch the rules
months later.

Your bracelet editor has three of them, and it already has a home for tests.

1. Open `homework/bracelet-tests` and delete `e2e/add.e2e.ts` there too.

2. Create `e2e/bracelet.e2e.ts`:

   ```ts
   import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test';

   test('refuses a second letter cube in a row', async ({ page }) => {
     await page.goto('/');

     await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'A', exact: true }).click();
     await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'B', exact: true }).click();

     await expect(page.getByText('You need to add a spacer bead next!')).toBeVisible();
   });

   test('refuses a spacer bead on the empty string', async ({ page }) => {
     await page.goto('/');

     await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'rose' }).click();

     await expect(page.getByText('You need to add a letter cube next!')).toBeVisible();
   });

   test('warns about mixed colors once and then keeps quiet', async ({ page }) => {
     await page.goto('/');

     await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'A', exact: true }).click();
     await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'rose' }).click();
     await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'B', exact: true }).click();
     await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'mint' }).click();

     await expect(page.getByText('You are mixing spacer colors!')).toBeVisible();

     await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'C', exact: true }).click();
     await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'blue' }).click();

     await expect(page.getByText('You are mixing spacer colors!')).toBeHidden();
   });
   ```

3. Run `npm run test:e2e`:

   ```text
   Running 3 tests using 1 worker

     ✓  1 e2e/bracelet.e2e.ts:3:1 › refuses a second letter cube in a row (240ms)
     ✓  2 e2e/bracelet.e2e.ts:12:1 › refuses a spacer bead on the empty string (136ms)
     ✓  3 e2e/bracelet.e2e.ts:20:1 › warns about mixed colors once and then keeps quiet (307ms)

     3 passed (1.6s)
   ```

The letter buttons need `{ exact: true }` for the same reason the dog's Name
field did. A plain `A` also matches the accessible name of `aqua`, `sand`,
`lilac`, `peach`, and `Remove last`, so strict mode stops the run and prints
all six buttons, the letter cube included.

The color buttons carry no text at all. `getByRole('button', { name: 'rose' })`
finds one anyway, because you gave every color button an `aria-label` back in
the bracelet chapter. A test that reads the page the way a screen reader does
only works on a page that a screen reader can read, which is the payoff for
every `<label for>` and every `aria-label` you have written since the DOM part.

`toBeHidden()` is the mirror of `toBeVisible()`, and it is how the last
assertion proves the warning came exactly once. There is a matcher for the
state of a control too: `expect(locator).toBeDisabled()` passes while a button
is gray and unclickable.

`npm test` in this project still runs the Vitest tests that call `Bracelet`
directly, and those are the tests that pin down `addLetter` throwing a
`RuleError`. The three tests above prove something the unit tests cannot
reach: that the refusal actually arrives on the page, in the paragraph a
person is looking at.

## What a keyboard does that a mouse does not {#sec-testing-apps-keyboard}

Watch somebody who fills in forms all day. They type a first name, press Tab,
type a last name, and press Enter, and the mouse never moves. A receptionist in
a busy salon works exactly like that. Go back to `coursework/hairdresser` and
add that flow as a second test in `e2e/salon.e2e.ts`:

```ts
test('adds a human when you press Enter in the form', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  await page.getByLabel('First name').fill('Tom');
  await page.getByLabel('Last name').fill('Novak');
  await page.getByLabel('Last name').press('Enter');

  await expect(page.getByText('Now serving: 🧑 Tom Novak (short hair)')).toBeVisible();
});
```

`press` sends one key to whatever the locator points at, and `'Enter'` is the
name of that key. Run `npm run test:e2e`:

```text
  ✓  1 e2e/salon.e2e.ts:3:1 › serves the customers in the order they arrived (377ms)
  ✘  2 e2e/salon.e2e.ts:23:1 › adds a human when you press Enter in the form (5.1s)


  1) e2e/salon.e2e.ts:23:1 › adds a human when you press Enter in the form ─────────────────────────

    Error: expect(locator).toBeVisible() failed

    Locator: getByText('Now serving: 🧑 Tom Novak (short hair)')
    Expected: visible
    Timeout: 5000ms
    Error: element(s) not found

    Call log:
      - Expect "toBeVisible" with timeout 5000ms
      - waiting for getByText('Now serving: 🧑 Tom Novak (short hair)')
```

Five seconds of asking, and Tom never showed up. The test is right and the app
is wrong. Enter in a text field fires a `submit` event on the form around it
(@sec-forms-submit), and the Add a human section of your salon has no form in
it. Two `<div>`s, a checkbox, and a button with a click listener answer the
mouse and have nothing to say to the keyboard.

Open `index.html` and put a form around the human fields, with the button
inside it:

```html
<form id="humanForm">
  <div class="field">
    <label for="humanFirstName">First name</label>
    <input id="humanFirstName" type="text">
  </div>
  <div class="field">
    <label for="humanLastName">Last name</label>
    <input id="humanLastName" type="text">
  </div>
  <div class="checkbox-field">
    <input id="humanLongHair" type="checkbox">
    <label for="humanLongHair">Long hair</label>
  </div>
  <button type="submit">Add human</button>
</form>
```

The button lost its `id` and gained `type="submit"`, so `src/index.ts` looks up
the form instead of the button:

```ts
const humanForm = document.querySelector<HTMLFormElement>('#humanForm');
```

Change that name in the null check too, and turn the listener into a `submit`
listener whose first line is the one you have written since the forms chapter:

```ts
humanForm.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();

  const firstName = humanFirstName.value.trim();
  const lastName = humanLastName.value.trim();
  // the rest of the listener stays exactly as it was
```

Run the tests again:

```text
Running 2 tests using 1 worker

  ✓  1 e2e/salon.e2e.ts:3:1 › serves the customers in the order they arrived (382ms)
  ✓  2 e2e/salon.e2e.ts:23:1 › adds a human when you press Enter in the form (158ms)

  2 passed (1.4s)
```

The first test still passes without a single edit, because a click on a submit
button fires the same `submit` event. One listener now answers the mouse and
the keyboard, and five lines of test found something that clicking through the
app by hand never did.

## Both kinds of test on every push {#sec-testing-apps-ci}

`npm run verify` runs the type check, Biome, and Vitest, and it has never
started a browser. That stays that way. Your 16 Vitest tests in the salon
project finish in 183 milliseconds, while the four Playwright tests need 1.8
seconds plus the time Vite takes to start, and `verify` is the command you run
before every commit. Speed is what makes you run it.

GitHub has no such worry. The workflow already runs after every push, nobody
waits for it, and a run that takes two minutes instead of one costs you
nothing. So the end-to-end tests go there.

Open `.github/workflows/verify.yml` in the root of your `creative-coding-2`
repository and add two steps at the end of the `bracelet-tests` job:

```yaml
  bracelet-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: homework/bracelet-tests
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: homework/bracelet-tests/package-lock.json
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run verify
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: npm run test:e2e
```

Everything above `npm run verify` is the file you wrote in the CI chapter, and
it does what it did there: fresh Linux machine, your repository downloaded onto
it, Node installed, packages installed with `npm ci`, and then your own check
command.

`npx playwright install --with-deps chromium` puts a browser on that machine.
`npm ci` installed the `@playwright/test` package, which is the program that
drives a browser, and the browser itself is a separate download of a few
hundred megabytes that npm knows nothing about. On your laptop you did this
once and forgot about it. The GitHub machine is thrown away after every run, so
this line runs every time. The word `chromium` at the end names the only
browser your `playwright.config.ts` asks for, so the other two stay
undownloaded. What `--with-deps` adds is your research task below.

`npm run test:e2e` is the same command you ran in your terminal. Playwright
starts Vite itself through the `webServer` block, drives the browser with no
window on the screen, and ends with an exit code. Red exit code, red cross next
to your commit.

The order matters. `verify` costs seconds and catches every type error and
every broken unit test, so it runs before the browser download. A commit that
does not compile fails in twenty seconds instead of two minutes.

::: {.research title="One flag and one picture"}
The exercise pushes an end-to-end job of your own, and then it breaks the app
on purpose and asks you to look at the page the test gave up on. Neither
answer is above. Playwright's page about continuous integration and its page
about browsers cover the first question, and its page about test configuration
covers the second.

1. `npx playwright install` downloads browsers. `--with-deps` does something
   more. What does the flag add, and why does a fresh GitHub machine need it
   while your own laptop never asked for it? Say where you read it.
2. Playwright can save a picture of the page at the moment a test fails.
   Which setting in `playwright.config.ts` switches that on, and which folder
   does the file land in? Say where you read it.

For the exam, remember why the browser step exists at all. A workflow that
installs packages and then runs Playwright without it fails on a machine that
has no browser, and the log line that says so is easy to miss.
:::

## Exercise: the salon under test {#sec-testing-apps-exercise}

Your `coursework/hairdresser` project has two end-to-end tests and a form that
answers the keyboard. This exercise finishes the suite and puts it on GitHub.

1. Open `coursework/hairdresser` and add a third test to `e2e/salon.e2e.ts`,
   called `'starts with an empty line and a dead Serve next button'`. It goes
   to `/` and touches nothing, then checks three things about the fresh page:
   `The line is empty.` is visible, so is `Customers in line: 0`, and the Serve
   next button is disabled.

2. Add a fourth test, `'refuses a human without a name'`. It clicks Add human
   with both name fields empty, then checks that
   `Please enter a first name and a last name.` is visible and that the line is
   still showing `The line is empty.`. The second assertion is the important
   one: a message that appears while the customer joins anyway is worse than no
   message.

3. Run `npm run test:e2e`:

   ```text
   Running 4 tests using 1 worker

     ✓  1 e2e/salon.e2e.ts:3:1 › serves the customers in the order they arrived (366ms)
     ✓  2 e2e/salon.e2e.ts:23:1 › adds a human when you press Enter in the form (129ms)
     ✓  3 e2e/salon.e2e.ts:33:1 › starts with an empty line and a dead Serve next button (104ms)
     ✓  4 e2e/salon.e2e.ts:41:1 › refuses a human without a name (134ms)

     4 passed (1.8s)
   ```

   Your line numbers and times differ. The four names and the green ticks do
   not.

4. Add the `verify` script with its three checks to `package.json` if the
   project has none yet, and run `npm run verify`. The 16 Vitest tests from the
   queues chapter have to be green as well.

5. Switch on the failure pictures your second research answer describes. It is
   one line in `playwright.config.ts`, inside the `use` block next to
   `baseURL`.

6. Break the app on purpose. In `src/index.ts`, change the message
   `'Please enter a first name and a last name.'` to anything else and run
   `npm run test:e2e`. Expected result: three green ticks, one cross on
   `refuses a human without a name`, and a line in the failure report naming
   the file Playwright saved:

   ```text
       attachment #1: screenshot (image/png) ──────────────────────────────
       test-results/salon.e2e.ts-refuses-a-human-without-a-name/test-failed-1.png
   ```

7. Open that PNG. Expected result: your salon page with the wrong message in
   it, exactly as the browser had it when the assertion gave up. Put the
   original message back and run the tests until they are green again.

8. Give the salon its own job in `.github/workflows/verify.yml`. Copy the whole
   `bracelet-tests:` block, name the copy `hairdresser:`, and point both of its
   paths at `coursework/hairdresser`. Keep the two Playwright steps.

9. Commit and push. Expected result: two lines in the Actions tab, one per job,
   both green after a minute or two. Open the `hairdresser` job and read the
   Playwright step. It prints the same four test names your terminal printed.

10. Break the same message once more, commit, and push. Expected result: a red
    cross next to the commit, and the log of the failing step naming
    `refuses a human without a name`. Put the message back, run
    `npm run verify` and `npm run test:e2e` until both are green, then commit
    and push, and leave the workflow file in your repository.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

**Test the dog form too.** The Add a dog section still has no form around it,
so Enter does nothing there either. Give it the same treatment and prove it
with a fifth test.

**Test the beehive.** Your beehive game from the SVG part sits on the plain
starter, which has no Playwright in it. Create a new app from the tests
template, copy your `src/` and `index.html` into it, and write one test that
presses `ArrowRight` twice and then expects `Bee at column 2, row 0.` on the
status line. `page.keyboard.press('ArrowRight')` sends the key to the page, and
your `keydown` listener sits on `document`, so it hears it without anything
being clicked first. Add a second test that walks the bee into the left wall
and proves it stays at column 0.

**Count what is on the page.** The salon shows Now serving and Next up and
nothing about the customers behind them. Render the rest of the line into an
`<ol>`, then assert how many list items stand there after four customers
joined. `getByRole('listitem')` finds them all at once, and Playwright's page
about assertions has the matcher for a number of elements.
:::
